extracted.intended_audience: novelists and fiction writers planning or revising novels
extracted.subtask_short: plotting novels with Save the Cat
extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide for novelists on applying the Save the Cat 15-beat structure to outline or revise a novel, with definitions of each beat, approximate placement, and usage tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening Image
rubrics_metrics.description: The Opening Image is your novel’s first snapshot of the main character’s world. Readers are seeing who your protagonist is before everything changes. What does their life look like? What feels normal to them? What’s missing, broken, or quietly off? Think of it as the 'before' picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approx. location: 0–1%. Purpose: show the protagonist's 'before' emotional state and world so readers have something to compare against later. Don’t over-explain; let readers feel the imbalance. This should set up contrast with the Final Image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme Stated
rubrics_metrics.description: The Theme Stated beat gives readers a hint about what your protagonist needs to learn. Usually this comes from another character—someone says something the protagonist doesn’t fully understand yet, ignores, or rejects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approx. location: ~5%. Tone: not a lecture or heavy-handed signposting; plant the idea like a seed. Beware of overdoing this—trust readers to pick up the theme without a billboard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup
rubrics_metrics.description: The Setup introduces your protagonist’s ordinary world. We learn what they want, what they’re avoiding, what they’re afraid of, and why their life can’t stay the same. Important supporting characters, early conflicts, and details that will matter later are introduced here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approx. location: 1–10%. Make setup feel like story—show the protagonist making choices, dealing with problems, wanting things—rather than dumping background. Avoid a slow opening that just 'clears its throat'; the story should already be moving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalyst
rubrics_metrics.description: The Catalyst is the moment that knocks the story off its normal track: a death, discovery, invitation, threat, betrayal, or strange opportunity that cracks the protagonist’s old normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approx. location: ~10%. It should matter and make the story click into gear; after it, the story shouldn’t simply return to business as usual. It doesn’t have to be spectacularly large in scale, but it must be disruptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate
rubrics_metrics.description: After the Catalyst, the protagonist hesitates—this is the Debate beat. They weigh options, resist, rationalize, or try to return to normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approx. location: 10–20%. Purpose: show why the forthcoming choice is hard and believable. Avoid instant, unrealistic commitment; readers should understand the stakes and reasons for hesitation even if they anticipate the choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break Into Two
rubrics_metrics.description: The Break Into Two is the point where your protagonist enters Act II and the new world of the story. They stop debating and step into the path they’ll follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approx. location: ~20%. Can be a literal threshold (leave home, enter new city) or an internal decision (accepting a truth). It should feel like a door closing—the old rules no longer apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: B Story
rubrics_metrics.description: The B Story is the secondary thread that helps carry the emotional weight of the novel. Often a romance, friendship, mentorship, rivalry, or family relationship that reveals what the protagonist must learn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approx. location: ~22%. The B Story usually supplies the emotional lesson that enables the protagonist’s final change; ignoring it risks having plot without heart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fun and Games
rubrics_metrics.description: Fun and Games is the part of the novel where the reader gets the thing they came for—the 'promise of the premise.' If the book is about a magical school, we need to experience the magical school; if it’s a mystery, the investigation should begin producing clues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approx. location: 20–50%. Deliver on the hook and genre expectations. 'Fun' here can be dark, dangerous, or terrifying depending on genre. This section must make readers feel the premise is being fulfilled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: The Midpoint happens around the middle of the story and must change the direction of the novel—often framed as a false victory or a false defeat that forces the protagonist to see things differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approx. location: ~50%. This beat must genuinely alter the story’s trajectory (stakes, goals, or approach) rather than simply being a big event. A strong Midpoint charges the second half of the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad Guys Close In
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad Guys Close In is when pressure tightens—external antagonists, internal flaws, systems, secrets, deadlines, or self-sabotage begin to constrict the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approx. location: 50–75%. The outside problems and inside problems should squeeze together, narrowing options and raising the cost of every choice. The story should increasingly feel like escape is harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: All Is Lost
rubrics_metrics.description: All Is Lost is the low point where the protagonist loses something important enough that the goal feels out of reach; sometimes literal (death, betrayal) and sometimes internal (loss of belief, identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approx. location: ~75%. Often includes a 'whiff of death' (metaphorical or literal). The loss must feel personal and consequential—if the reader shrugs, the beat is failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark Night of the Soul
rubrics_metrics.description: The Dark Night of the Soul is the fallout from the All Is Lost moment—an emotional pause where the protagonist sits with failure, grief, confusion, shame, or fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approx. location: 75–80%. This is the pause before the final turn; it needs to land emotionally. Don’t rush it—this moment sets up the clarity that enables the Break Into Three.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break Into Three
rubrics_metrics.description: The Break Into Three is the moment of clarity when the protagonist finally understands what they must do and who they need to become to succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approx. location: ~80%. Frequently the lesson from the B Story clicks here and emotional and plot threads align, giving the protagonist a new way forward (plan, courage, resolve).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale
rubrics_metrics.description: The Finale is where the protagonist faces the central conflict one last time—this is the climax, testing whether they have truly changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approx. location: 80–99%. The outcome should flow naturally from character growth and prior choices—avoid random solutions, deus ex machina, or 'it was in a drawer' endings. Whether the protagonist wins or loses, the result must be earned by their arc and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Image
rubrics_metrics.description: The Final Image is the last snapshot of the protagonist’s world and should mirror the Opening Image to show what has changed—strength, freedom, loss, peace, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approx. location: 99–100%. Purpose: show the 'after' without overexplaining. Give one final emotional note and get out of the way—avoid winks or explicit moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to use Save the Cat while writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-guidance on using the beat sheet: treat it like a map, not a rulebook. Use it for outlining or revision; the beats help reveal where a draft is losing momentum and what kind of shift a scene must produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: • Don’t treat beats as a checkbox exercise—avoid inserting beats superficially. • Percentages are rough guides, not strict rules ('they’re not the boss of you'). • A beat is a turn: ask 'Does this moment change the story?' rather than 'Do I have an event here?' • Use beats before drafting if you’re an outliner (sketch Catalyst, Break Into Two, Midpoint, All Is Lost, Finale first); discovery writers can use them as a revision tool to diagnose problems (e.g., weak Midpoint, unearned ending, B Story lacking emotional weight). • Typical diagnostic questions from the page: Does the beginning show who the protagonist is before change? Does the Catalyst actually disrupt their life? Does the Midpoint change the direction or just add noise? Does the ending feel earned? • Use beats to find structural issues (slow middle, rushed ending, low emotional stakes) and to make changes that cause genuine turns rather than superficial events.
